subtype: Reskilling & Career Change in an AI Era
passage: I'm Deepika, and I've shared a flat with Vasudha for three years. She was a translator. Last year her work almost dried up; clients said software could do a first draft. For a few weeks she barely left her room. Then one morning she was up at six with a notebook. She'd listed what software still got wrong: legal nuance, tone, cultural meaning. She signed up for an evening course in legal translation and another on checking machine output. Some nights she came home grey-faced and complained that it was like being a student again at twenty-five. I don't know if she was scared; she didn't say much. But she kept going. Now she reviews contracts for a law firm, and she's busy.

qa.q: What did Vasudha work as before her work dried up?
qa.a: She was a translator.

qa.q: What does Vasudha barely leaving her room for weeks suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt shaken and low when her work suddenly disappeared.

qa.q: What made Vasudha's retraining well aimed?
qa.a: She studied what software still got wrong and trained specifically in those areas, like legal nuance and checking machine output.

qa.q: How does Deepika see Vasudha's change?
qa.a: Deepika admires Vasudha's persistence but admits not knowing exactly how scared Vasudha felt.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young translator deliberately retrain as her industry shifted.

subtype: Reskilling & Career Change in an AI Era
passage:
January: Parveen's call-centre team was told half their queries would now go to an automated assistant. She went home and told her sister Sharmila she felt replaceable.

March: She had started a weekend course in data analysis. The first assignment took her six hours and she nearly quit. Sharmila found her asleep on the laptop and made her tea.

August: Parveen applied for an internal role analysing where the automated assistant failed customers. In the interview she explained which complaints the machine mishandled, from her own years on calls. She got it. On her first day she messaged Sharmila: 'Still scared. But the good kind of scared.' Her salary was about the same. Her work felt like it had a future.

qa.q: What course did Parveen start by March?
qa.a: She started a weekend course in data analysis.

qa.q: What did Parveen mean by 'the good kind of scared'?
qa.a: She was still nervous about the new role but felt excited and hopeful rather than threatened.

qa.q: What helped Parveen's retraining lead to a job?
qa.a: She combined new analysis skills with her real knowledge of customer calls, which the role needed.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have seen these months?
qa.a: She watched her sister struggle and supported her quietly, so she likely felt relieved and proud by August. 🤍

grounding: Shows a young worker retraining over months to adapt when automation changed her job.

subtype: Reskilling & Career Change in an AI Era
passage: Ramesh, sit, I'll tell you something. When I was your age, twenty-four, I set type by hand in a printing press. Then computers came. My boss said, 'Learn or leave.' I was angry for a month. I thought, I'm skilled, why should a machine decide? My friend Alka had already joined night classes in computer typesetting. She dragged me along. I was the slowest in class, sitting between college boys. It was embarrassing. But I learned, and within two years I was teaching others at the press. Now you tell me your office is using these AI tools. Don't waste a month being angry like I did. Find out what the new thing can't do, and learn to do that well.

qa.q: What did the storyteller do at the printing press?
qa.a: The storyteller set type by hand.

qa.q: How did the storyteller feel sitting in the night class?
qa.a: The storyteller felt embarrassed, being the slowest and older than the college boys.

qa.q: What advice does the elder give Ramesh about AI tools?
qa.a: Don't stay angry; find out what the new tools can't do and get good at that.

qa.q: How might Alka have seen her friend's early anger?
qa.a: She probably understood it but pushed her friend anyway, knowing waiting would cost more.

grounding: Shows an elder passing on a lesson about deliberately retraining when technology changes work.

subtype: Reskilling & Career Change in an AI Era
passage: Gopika's translation orders had halved in a year. Clients now ran documents through AI tools and wanted her only to 'check' them, at a third of the price. At twenty-five, with rent due and her father's shop barely breaking even, she couldn't afford to stop working to retrain. So she carved out mornings: 6 to 7:30, before the checking jobs started, for an online course in UX writing. Arnab, her flatmate, lent her his old laptop when hers froze in the middle of an assignment. Some mornings she fell asleep over the modules. After four months she rewrote the menus of a local clinic's booking page for free, testing it with Arnab's grandmother, who kept tapping the wrong button. Gopika changed the words until she didn't. That small project got her first paid UX job. She still takes translation work. Just less of it.

qa.q: When did Gopika study for her course?
qa.a: From 6 to 7:30 in the mornings, before her checking jobs started.

qa.q: What does Gopika falling asleep over the modules suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She was exhausted from juggling paid work and retraining, yet determined enough to keep going.

qa.q: What made Gopika's retraining deliberate and effective?
qa.a: Protected daily study time, a practical free project tested with a real user, and keeping her old work while building the new skill.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Arnab's grandmother to test the booking page?
qa.a: Probably confusing at first, but her mistakes helped Gopika make the words clearer for people like her.

grounding: Shows a translator whose work is shrinking because of AI retraining deliberately for a new role despite money and time limits.

subtype: Reskilling & Career Change in an AI Era
passage: The memo at Karthik's Pune office said the reconciliation team would be 'restructured' in six months; software now did most of what he did. At twenty-six, he felt the floor tilt. He spent a weekend refreshing job sites and feeling sick. On Monday Sabina, a senior in the analytics team whom he had helped with data last year, found him in the cafeteria. 'You understand our transactions better than anyone. That's half of what we do. The other half is learnable.' She told him about the company's internal training programme and offered to review his practice work. Karthik signed up that week. Evenings went to spreadsheets, then a query language, then small dashboards built on anonymised data from his own team. It was humbling to be the slowest in the class. After five months he applied for a junior analyst opening, with Sabina as a reference. He got it.

qa.q: When would the reconciliation team be restructured?
qa.a: In six months.

qa.q: What does 'felt the floor tilt' show about Karthik's feelings?
qa.a: He felt shaken and insecure, as if his stable job had suddenly slipped from under him.

qa.q: How did Karthik turn the threat into a plan?
qa.a: He joined internal training, practised steadily on familiar data, took feedback from Sabina, and applied for a role that used his domain knowledge.

qa.q: Why might Sabina have chosen to help Karthik?
qa.a: She remembered his help last year and saw his knowledge of transactions as valuable to her team.

grounding: Shows an office worker whose role is being automated retraining deliberately into a new role with a colleague's support.
